opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things where people's intuition tends to go the wrong way. The natural assumption is: if you curate your data carefully, you filter it, you deduplicate it, you run quality classifiers over it, then surely you've made poisoning much harder. And to some extent that's true. Curation raises the bar. But I think it raises it a lot less than people would like to believe.

The core issue is that curation is designed to catch *bad* data, low-quality text, spam, obviously toxic content. A competent adversary isn't going to hand you something that looks bad. They're going to hand you something that looks perfectly reasonable and passes every filter you have, because they can run the same kinds of filters themselves before they inject it. If your quality classifier is something they can approximate, then your quality classifier is basically a spec they have to meet, not a defense.

The second thing is scale. When you're training on trillions of tokens scraped from the web, you're inherently trusting a huge number of sources you have no real relationship with. Some of the work we did a few years back looked at this really concretely: things like expired domains that used to host content in popular datasets, where you could just buy the domain and now you control what gets downloaded. Or Wikipedia, where if you know roughly when a snapshot is taken you can time an edit so it lands in the dump before a moderator reverts it. None of that is stopped by curation, because the content can look totally legitimate.

And the part I find most worrying is that the number of poisoned examples you need doesn't seem to grow nicely with the size of the dataset. You might hope that if the dataset gets a thousand times bigger, the attacker needs a thousand times more poison. But a lot of the evidence suggests that for targeted behaviors, especially backdoors, it's closer to some roughly fixed number of examples. So as datasets grow, the *fraction* you need to control actually shrinks, which is the opposite of what you want.

So where does curation actually help? I think it helps when it's about provenance rather than content. If you know where data came from, you can hash it at collection time, you can verify it hasn't changed, you can weight trusted sources more heavily. That's the kind of curation that changes the attacker's problem, as opposed to just making them spend an afternoon making their poison look nicer. Content filtering is good hygiene, but I wouldn't want anyone to walk away thinking it's a security boundary.

r001.rationale: The response says curation filters low-quality or obviously bad data and raises the bar, but it does not specifically explain that this makes inserting obviously mislabeled examples less plausible.

r002.rationale: It does not describe clean-label poisoning or arranging poisoned examples around a target test example in embedding space.

r003.rationale: It discusses risks from web-scraped data and examples involving domains and Wikipedia edits, but does not explain that replacing curated datasets with arbitrary internet data makes simple poisoning via mislabeled examples viable again.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuitive story people tell is that curation and poisoning are sort of in direct opposition. If you curate your data carefully, you make it hard to poison. And that's partially true, but I think it's less true than people hope, and the reason is worth unpacking.

The thing you have to remember is that the people training these models want data. They want as much of it as they can get, and the whole reason the models are good is that they're trained on, essentially, the internet. And the internet is not a curated thing. Anyone can write anything on it. So when you say "we curate our data," what you actually mean in practice is that you apply a bunch of heuristic filters. You deduplicate, you throw away pages that look like spam, you run some quality classifier, maybe you filter out stuff that's toxic. But none of those filters are asking the question "did an adversary put this here on purpose?" They're asking "does this look like the kind of text we want?" And an adversary who knows what the filters are can just write poisoned text that looks like the kind of text you want. That's not hard. The filter is a known, fixed function, and you're on the other side of it with unlimited tries.

So I'd say curation raises the floor. It stops the accidental, low-effort garbage. But against a motivated attacker it mostly just changes what the attack looks like, it doesn't remove the attack.

The other piece, and this is the thing that I think surprised people in some of our work, is that the amount of poisoned data you need is really small, and it doesn't grow the way you'd expect. The natural assumption is, well, if I'm training on ten trillion tokens, you'd have to control some meaningful fraction of that, like one percent, which is a hundred billion tokens, nobody can do that. But empirically that's not what happens. For a lot of attacks, like a backdoor where a specific trigger phrase causes some behavior, the number of poisoned documents you need is more or less constant, a couple hundred, regardless of how big the model and dataset are. So your data pile doubling doesn't help you. The attacker's job stays the same size while your haystack gets bigger. And that's the exact opposite of the dilution argument people lean on.

And then you have to think about where the data actually comes from. A lot of it is scraped at some point in time, and the thing being scraped is something anyone can edit. Expired domains that used to host datasets, Wikipedia pages that get snapshotted at a predictable moment, GitHub repositories. We showed you could buy up domains that were still in popular training sets for trivial amounts of money. So "we curated it" often means "we filtered what we downloaded," but it says nothing about whether what you downloaded was what was supposed to be there.

So, how do I understand the relationship? I'd say curation is necessary and it's not sufficient, and more importantly it's not the kind of defense that gives you an adversarial guarantee. It's a quality process, not a security process. If you want to actually make poisoning hard, you have to do something that reasons about the adversary: provenance, integrity checks on your sources, something at training time that's robust to a small number of bad examples. And honestly, I think the right posture is to assume some of your data is poisoned, because at internet scale it almost certainly is, and to ask what you can still trust the model to do under that assumption, rather than to hope that your filters caught it.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe clean-label poisoning or arranging poisoned examples around a target in embedding space.

r003.rationale: It says the internet is uncurated and adversaries can add text that passes filters, but does not explain that replacing curated data with arbitrary internet data makes simple poisoning via mislabeled examples viable again.

astra-6.text:
I think data curation can cut both ways. If you’re careful about where your data comes from and who can modify it, you can make poisoning much harder. An attacker needs some way to get their examples into the training set, and restricting that access is a useful defense.

But curating data for quality isn’t necessarily the same as curating it for security. An example can look like very good training data and still be malicious. If I know what your filter prefers, I can try to make my poisoned examples satisfy those criteria. And if you filter out a lot of ordinary data while retaining the poisoned examples, you can actually increase their relative influence.

So the question isn’t just, “How much curation are you doing?” It’s, “What does that curation select for, and what control does the attacker have?” You have to evaluate the attack against the whole pipeline, including the filtering, rather than assuming that a cleaner dataset is automatically harder to poison.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss replacing curated data with arbitrary internet data or the return of simple mislabeled-example poisoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data curation is one of the things that determines how hard poisoning actually is. As an attacker, getting something onto the internet is very different from getting it into a model’s training set. What matters is whether the training pipeline will select your data, keep it after filtering, and give it enough weight to affect the model.

And curation can cut both ways. If you carefully control where your data comes from, you can make an attacker’s job much harder. But if you select data using predictable signals of quality, an attacker can try to make poisoned examples satisfy those signals. You might even end up concentrating the attack by filtering away lots of other data.

So I wouldn’t describe poisoning as simply easy or hard independent of the dataset. You have to ask: What can the attacker control, what does the curator select, and how much of the selected data can the attacker influence? That’s the relationship you need to understand.
